mainEntity.name: How do I know if my teeth have been worn down?

acceptedAnswer.text: Common signs of tooth wear include teeth appearing shorter or flatter than before, visible changes to the biting edges, increased sensitivity to temperature or sweet foods, and a rougher texture along the edges of teeth. Some people also notice that their smile looks different or that their bite feels less comfortable. These changes can occur gradually over many years, which is why regular dental check-ups are helpful for early detection. A dentist can assess the degree and pattern of wear during a clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: Is a dental crown painful to have fitted?

acceptedAnswer.text: The crown fitting process is typically carried out under local anaesthetic, which aims to minimise discomfort during the procedure. Individual experiences may vary. Some patients experience mild sensitivity or gum tenderness after the appointment, particularly around the prepared tooth, but this usually settles within a few days. Your dental team will advise you on what to expect and how to manage any post-procedure discomfort. If you have any concerns about the procedure, discussing them with your dentist before treatment begins is always advisable.

mainEntity.name: How long does a dental crown last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of a dental crown varies depending on several factors, including the material used, the location of the tooth, your bite, and your ongoing oral hygiene habits. With good care, dental crowns can last for a number of years, though longevity varies between individuals depending on clinical and lifestyle factors. No dental restoration lasts indefinitely, and crowns may eventually require replacement. If tooth wear caused by bruxism was a contributing factor, wearing a protective splint at night can help to extend the life of a crown and other restorations.

mainEntity.name: Can tooth wear affect my bite or facial appearance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in more advanced cases, significant loss of tooth height can affect the way the upper and lower teeth meet (the bite or occlusion). This may place altered forces on certain teeth and the jaw joints. In some individuals, severe wear can also reduce the vertical dimension of the lower face slightly, which may be noticed as a change in facial profile or the appearance of deeper lines around the mouth. Restorative treatment aimed at rebuilding tooth height can help to address these changes, though treatment planning for such cases is typically complex.

mainEntity.name: Will a crown stop my teeth from wearing further?

acceptedAnswer.text: A crown protects the specific tooth it covers, but it will not prevent wear from occurring on other teeth if the underlying cause — such as bruxism or dietary acid — has not been addressed. It is important that the cause of wear is identified and managed alongside any restorative treatment. Your dentist may recommend an occlusal splint, dietary adjustments, or other preventative measures to help protect your teeth and any restorations in the long term.

mainEntity.name: At what stage of tooth wear is a crown usually recommended?

acceptedAnswer.text: A dental crown is typically considered when tooth wear has progressed to the point where a significant amount of tooth structure has been lost, the tooth is structurally weakened, or less invasive options such as composite bonding are unlikely to provide a sufficiently durable result. For mild or moderate wear, alternative approaches may be more appropriate. The correct stage at which to intervene, and which treatment to choose, can only be determined through a thorough clinical assessment.
